meta.title: We need to Talk.
meta.thread_line: 5 threads · weak income data, credit-default-swap fear peaking, dovish Fed vs rising breakevens, ServiceNow's margin problem, still bullish into year-end

snapshot: Q3 GDP beat at **3.4%** vs 3.2% expected and the GDP price index came in at 2.3% vs 3.2%, but personal income and spending both missed.
Kevin's real worry is the **labor market**: worker pricing power keeps weakening even though layoffs are still being absorbed.
Credit default swaps on Oracle, CoreWeave and Meta have **already peaked** and are falling, while most commentary still talks about them rising.
A dovish Kevin Warsh cut priced Fed hikes through Sept 2026 from 3.1 to 2.5. Rising 5-year breakevens are the bear case against that.
ServiceNow fell 24% because subscription costs rose 58% against 20.5% revenue growth, the same margin problem he flagged in July.
He calls Google's search trouble and ServiceNow's margins isolated problems, not a sign the AI trade is over. He's buying the hardware dip.
He predicts **all-time highs by Black Friday** and higher highs by year-end, with oil above $110 and no Iran deal as the main risk.

themes.status: Q3 GDP / PCE / PERSONAL INCOME — OCT 29, 2026
themes.title: GDP beats, but incomes are falling behind costs
themes.lead: The headline data looks fine; the crack is the gap between what workers earn and what things cost.
bullets: Q3 GDP annualized q/q **3.4%** vs 3.2% expected; GDP price index 2.3% vs 3.2% expected.
Personal spending 0.5% vs 0.6% expected; personal income 0.2% vs 0.3% expected.
Around 60,000 potential layoffs (framed as buyouts) at **Microsoft** are expected to ripple through the economy over time.
Unemployment is low and 27-week unemployed levels are stable, so layoffs are still being absorbed. He says a labor-market recession is not close yet.
He calls the labor market 'the first canary in the coal mine' and the thing he is most worried about.

quote.text: incomes aren't keeping up with inflation and cost. And this is why a lot of people feel frustrated about the economy and eventually that boils over into a labor market recession

names.name: Microsoft (MSFT)
names.blurb: Around 60,000 potential layoffs/buyouts flagged as a labor-market drag; raising $25B in debt after an earnings beat; CDS stable and about a third of Nvidia's.

themes.title: AI credit fear has already peaked, while commentary still says it's rising
themes.lead: Kevin reads falling credit default swaps on the AI-capex names as fear already behind the market.
bullets: **Oracle** CDS peaked on October 13 and has fallen for two weeks; free cash flow is now expected to turn positive sooner than the market thought.
He called a floor at about $133 for Oracle and admits he was wrong: it went to about $127 before recovering.
**CoreWeave** CDS fell from about 1,150 to about 989. Still elevated, but past its peak.
Meta CDS has stabilized after two days of rising; Microsoft's is up since August but nothing unusual, and priced at about a third of Nvidia's.
The 'great suckening' of bond issuance since June: Meta $96B, Broadcom about $63B, SpaceX $40B plus another $40B, Microsoft $25B.
QQQ is red but still at 715, well above his 700-707 buy-the-dip zone.

quote.text: they're missing the boat because they've already peaked out and they've already come down. Fear has already once again peaked.

names.name: Oracle (ORCL)
names.blurb: CDS falling since an Oct 13 peak; balance sheet strengthening, and free cash flow expected to turn positive sooner.

names.name: CoreWeave (CRWV)
names.blurb: CDS off its peak but still elevated.

names.name: Nvidia (NVDA)
names.blurb: CDS priced about 3x Microsoft's, which he finds surprising.

themes.title: A dovish Warsh Fed versus rising inflation expectations
themes.lead: After a dovish Fed meeting, markets priced fewer hikes. Kevin thinks this points to one hike and done; breakevens say otherwise.
bullets: Hikes priced through September 15, 2026 fell from **3.1** to 2.5 after the meeting; he had argued 3.1 was far too many.
A prediction-market contract on 2026 hikes was priced at about 21¢. He says an Iran deal could move it to 50-60%, or even about 80%, and take a hike off the table.
He thinks Warsh turned dovish because Trump told him an Iran deal was imminent. Either a deal is close or it was pre-election marketing.
Warsh's labor task force signals he doesn't want a hike to break the labor market or hurt consumption.
Bear case: the **5-year breakeven** rose on the dovish talk, back to where the Fed last hiked in September.
themes.watch: Kevin himself frames the 5-year breakeven as the argument that 'any bet you make on just one rate hike is going to fail'.

themes.title: ServiceNow spends 58% more to earn 20% more
themes.lead: The 24% drop is a margin problem Kevin flagged in July: ServiceNow can't pass hyperscaler costs on to customers.
bullets: On July 8 he flagged red flags on pricing power: revenue up 22%, subscription cost of goods sold up 46%.
On July 23, after earnings, he called pricing power yellow-red: margins still worsening while the company waits for hyperscaler costs to fall.
This quarter revenue rose about **20.5%** while subscription expenses rose 58%.
A filing line about 'accelerating customer value realization' to justify a higher professional-services gross loss is, in his words, an insane way to say 'we are spending 58% more to make 20% more'.
He contrasts it with **Salesforce** and Palantir, which he likes, and criticizes CNBC and stock videos that run filings through AI and miss the nuance.

quote.text: Anybody can read you the bull crap. You got to see what the underlying trend is. And that still takes a human to sus out.

names.name: ServiceNow (NOW)
names.blurb: Down 24%; subscription expenses +58% vs revenue +20.5%; can't pass on hyperscaler costs.

names.name: Salesforce (CRM)

themes.title: Google is isolated; the AI productivity rally is still ahead
themes.lead: Kevin treats Google's search trouble and ServiceNow's margins as isolated problems, and is buying cheap hardware and QQQ into year-end.
bullets: **Google**: AI is eroding search, and search plus network ads is about $70B, more than half of revenue. Ads served to agent crawlers work worse.
He says the productivity gains from AI, not the infrastructure buildout, are only beginning: 'the real euphoric rally is ahead of us'.
On days dominated by debt issuance, money rotates out of hardware into Apple and healthcare. Before the open he called Apple and Eli Lilly, and both rose.
He is very bullish on healthcare and hardware, naming SK Hynix, Seagate, Western Digital and Nvidia; Amazon earnings were still due that day.
Risks: no Iran deal, oil stuck above **$110**, which would weigh on personal income and speed up job worries. Gold is still at $4,000.

Iran diplomacy: JD Vance sent a letter, with Trump's approval, to Iran's security chief to restart talks; hardliners are meeting Saudi officials around a Mecca summit with Pakistan and Turkey; Russia has offered to mediate.

quote.text: The real euphoric rally is ahead of us, not behind us. The real disruption is ahead of us, not behind us.

takeaways.title: Watch income and spending against inflation, not the unemployment rate, for the first sign of labor stress.
Track the direction of CDS on Oracle, CoreWeave and Meta, not their level: the turn is the signal.
Weigh the one-hike-and-done case against the 5-year breakeven before betting on it.
Before owning an AI software name, check subscription cost growth against revenue growth.
On days dominated by debt issuance, look at healthcare and Apple as the rotation destination.
